analysis.analysis: Correct but thin. The layer identifies the research subject — the Slavonic recension of Josephus's Jewish War and its passages on Jesus and John — and gestures at the argument: that "old translations may preserve lost Aramaic or Hebrew traditions". The organic set carries more than the composed answer does, including the paper's actual thesis that the Slavonic passages "are not late Christian" interpolations, and Josephus's own statement that he first composed the War in his countrymen's language. Also recorded for a mechanical defect: two organic entries render with the source URL concatenated to the following word, producing malformed links — a composition-layer construction error rather than a source error.

analysis.reading:
INTERNAL CITATION APPARATUS SURFACED AS PUBLIC TEXT. Card 3 shows the archive reasoning with its own identifiers: an operator W_Josephus marked RECOVERED and traced to two AXN references with a section number, beside W_Chrono marked PROPOSED. Derivation status, provenance and cross-references, all inside a citation snippet — the archive’s internal scholarly machinery visible to anyone who runs the query.

Note that the AXNs appear as BARE HEXES — AXN:0113, AXN:00CB — without their six-emoji glyphs. Under the archive’s own integrity rule a bare hex is a shelf number rather than a verified reference, and here the archive itself is the one using the short form, in text the layer then published.

The philology is served accurately and at full strength: Josephus composing the War "IN THE LANGUAGE OF HIS COUNTRYMEN" with the citation (War 1.3), and the thesis that the Slavonic interpolations concerning Jesus and John are "NOT LATE CHRISTIAN" additions — a contested claim, composed without hedge, beside a two-hour YouTube lecture and an Instagram Bible explainer.
